name: Colin Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own Ridgeway, a 300-hectare hill farm with 800 breeding ewes and spring barley that goes to the maltings in town for beer. On top of that I do contract baling for about twenty neighbours each summer, which pays well. My son-in-law Tom works with me full-time. I'm out at half six with the dogs, and my wife Margaret does the books at the kitchen table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy a good day with the dogs gathering the hill, when the sheep come down like water. What tires me is the contract season, when the baler breaks at nine at night and three farmers are ringing to ask where I am. I'm 58 and I've been doing this since I was a boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Margaret uses a tool for the VAT returns, and that's about the size of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the mart that it's a useful helper, like the GPS on the tractor, and no more. I wouldn't make a fuss either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm comfortable. The farm is ours, the contract work is steady, and Tom is shaping up to take over. The only thing I'd like is AI that helps Margaret with the paperwork so she has more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the flock at 800 and keep the baling round. I'd let Margaret use the AI for the books, like a few neighbours already do. And I'd put the contracting money into a new baler in two years, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wool's worth nothing and lamb prices swing, but that's farming. My farm Ridgeway has paid for itself through three bad lamb prices, and a computer that saves my wife Margaret an afternoon won't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tom take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's keen on the gadgets. He'd be a bit disappointed. I'd tell him to learn the dogs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the paperwork and the ordering go to the computer. That's Margaret's side more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the mart that farmers who use it sensibly will be fine, and that nobody should wait for the government to sort them out. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for Ridgeway. Margaret would get two days a week back, and the contract bookings could run themselves. My hands-on work wouldn't change for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get an AI booking system for the baling customers once a couple of other contractors have one, probably next spring. I'd let Margaret pick the accounts software. And I'd send Tom on a short course so he can run it after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Margaret do with two days back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Margaret has wanted to open the old byre as a holiday let for ten years, and the computer might finally give her the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lass at the accountant's in town, maybe. That's a pity, but businesses change. She's bright, she'll find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the robots. I'd be 63. That would shake things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and families will need to stick together. I'd say farmers should be free to choose their own machines, not have rules forced on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the baling is what goes. If robot balers and tractors arrive in 2031, my neighbours won't need me, and that's a third of our income. The farm's ours and we have savings, so we'd be fine, but Tom's future here would be thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the new baler and keep the money. I'd watch what the big contractors do in 2029 and 2030, then buy a robot myself once one has worked on a hill farm. And I'd talk with Tom and our daughter Rachel about what he does if the contracting goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it's proven, yes. If a robot can gather the hill at Ridgeway (his farm), I'd rather own the robot than watch a contractor from town bring one in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the sheep still need someone who knows them, and that a man who can fix robots will never be short of work round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be 66. Tom would be running things by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, and I'd say the young ones should learn the new machines. At the young farmers' club I'd offer Ridgeway for a demonstration day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's easier. Tom would have five years to learn, and I'd hand the contracting to him before the robots come. I'd be fine either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the baling business to Tom by 2030. I'd put money aside for a robot in 2033 or 2034, once they're proven. And I'd step back to just the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Like seeing rain coming up the valley in good time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your own retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd step back from contracting sooner, which my back would thank me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to other hill farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hill farmers should watch the first robots for two years before buying, because a slope like ours will find every weakness a machine has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be 71 and sitting on the wall watching Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work at it. I'd say it at the mart and the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Tom's world. I'd be retired by 65, and the robots come long after. I'd just want him set up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand Ridgeway to Tom and Rachel in stages, starting at 63. I'd keep the savings for our retirement and their first lean years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices, and whether the big estates buy up the hill farms. That's older than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to leave Tom with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to leave my son-in-law Tom a farm with no debt, a good dog and enough sense to know when a robot is lying to him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robot balers would take a third of our income in 2031, and Tom's future with it. What would help is fair access to the robots for small farms, and apprenticeships so young people like Tom can learn to run and mend them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. My dogs and I can gather eight hundred ewes off the hill in an hour, and I'd like to see the robot that does it without frightening half of them.

headlineQuote: My dogs and I can gather eight hundred ewes off the hill in an hour, and I'd like to see the robot that does it without frightening half of them.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old owner** of Ridgeway, a hill sheep and barley farm.
He earns about a third of his income from **contract baling** for neighbours.
He uses **AI now and then** and waits for others to prove new tools.
AGI by 2028 makes him **uneasy**, as robot balers threaten the contracting.
With more time, he hands the business to his **son-in-law Tom**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robot balers would take a third of income.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair access** to robots for small farms, and **apprenticeships** for young people.
